title: Lost updates: row locks, SKIP LOCKED and job queues
goal: By the end, you can spot the read, compute, write pattern that loses updates and stop it four ways, build a to-do list of jobs that many workers share without waiting or doing a job twice, and keep two transfers from waiting for each other forever.
opening:
Picture the company behind a coffee-shop payments app, checking its numbers at the month's end. Ivy's spending account started the month at 50.00. On the first morning, in one second, two charges were taken from it: 10.00 for a coffee and a 10.00 monthly fee. It should show 30.00. It shows 40.00.

Both charges are in the list of payments, and both programs reported success, with no error anywhere. The company is ten dollars short.

It's easy to think the database prevents this: it made the second charge wait until the first was saved. Waiting your turn feels safe, and in a test that sends one charge at a time, it is.

In What a transaction promises, two payments broke a rule over Ivy's two accounts. This time both touch one account, the simplest race there is. In this lesson, we'll lose that update on purpose and fix it four ways. Then we'll share a to-do list among several programs, and make two transfers wait for each other forever. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Two programs each take 1,000 cents (10.00) from Ivy's account 109, which holds 5,000, at the same moment, with the database's default settings. Each reads the balance, subtracts 1,000 in its own Kotlin code, then writes the result back with `UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = :computed`. The second write waits until the first is saved. What is the balance when both are done?
options: 3,000: the wait made the two charges take turns
4,000: one charge is lost
5,000: the second transaction undoes the first
The second write fails with an error
warmup.why: Both read 5,000 before either wrote, and each worked out 4,000 in its own code. The wait put the two writes in order, but the value the second one wrote was decided before it waited, so it wrote over the first charge: a lost update. The first option is the trap: waiting puts writes in order, and it doesn't redo the subtraction. An error would come at a stricter level, Repeatable Read, and the default isn't that.

sections.h: Read, compute, write: two charges and one lost update
sections.body:
Let's put the scene from the opening into the database. The company keeps its data in PostgreSQL, a free database program, in tables made of rows. Each of Ivy's accounts is one row of the `accounts` table, and its `balance_minor` column holds the balance in cents, so 5,000 is 50.00. Two programs take money from account 109 at the same moment: one for a card payment of 1,000, one for a monthly fee of 1,000. Each works inside a transaction, a group of statements that the database applies together or not at all. And each does the same three things: it reads the balance, subtracts in its own Kotlin code, and writes the result.

```kotlin
val balance = selectBalance(109)        // 5000
updateBalance(109, balance - 1000)      // SET balance_minor = 4000
```

Run them one after the other, and the balance ends at 3,000. Now let them overlap. Both read 5,000. The payment writes 4,000 and commits, which makes its change permanent. The fee writes 4,000 and commits. Two charges ran, and one left no trace. This is a **lost update**: two transactions read the same value, each writes a result worked out from it, and the second write erases the first. Nothing failed, so no log line tells you.

The pattern is called a read-modify-write cycle: read a value, work out a new one in the program, and write it back. It hides in more places than balances. A counter of likes does it. So does a program that loads a whole document, changes one field and saves all of it back. So does a worker that reads which job is next and then marks it taken, which the fourth section comes back to.

PostgreSQL saw the overlap and couldn't help. An UPDATE puts a row lock on every row it changes: a mark that makes any other writer of that row wait until this transaction commits or rolls back. So the fee's UPDATE waited for the payment's commit. Then it went ahead with the value it had been given, 4,000, worked out from a read that was no longer true. The lock put the two writes in order. It couldn't fix a number the program had worked out from an old read.

The simulator runs the broken version. You pick which transaction takes its next step. Each transaction's UPDATE and COMMIT are one step there, so, as in PostgreSQL, nobody ever reads a value that isn't committed yet. Try to lose a charge. Then we'll take the arithmetic out of the program's hands.

sim.title: Two debits of 1,000 on account 109
sim.intro: Each transaction reads the balance, subtracts 1,000 in its Kotlin code, then writes the result and commits in one step. Pick who runs next. Can you end with balance = 4000?

goal.say: Lost update: two charges ran, and the balance fell by 1,000. Both read 5,000 before either wrote. In PostgreSQL the second UPDATE would also have waited for the first one's row lock, and that changes nothing: its value was worked out from the old read. Let one transaction finish before the other reads, and you get 3,000.

steps: Open two terminals in the `labs` folder and run psql, PostgreSQL's program for typing SQL, in both: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course`. Call them A and B. Each is one session, an open connection to the database, like one of the two programs. Start the database first if it isn't running (`docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`).
Run the first block, switching terminals where the comments say (`-- A` or `-- B`). B's UPDATE hangs: it's waiting for A's row lock. Run A's COMMIT and watch B's UPDATE finish.

code.title: psql, two sessions on database course

try.expect:
Both SELECTs show 5000. B's first UPDATE prints nothing: it's waiting for the lock A took on row 109. The moment A commits, B's UPDATE finishes:

```postgresql
-- B, after A's COMMIT
UPDATE 1
COMMIT
-- A

---------------
          4000
(1 row)
```

Two charges, and the balance went down by 1,000. B waited for A and still wrote over A's work, because the value 4000 was decided before the wait. In the second version B waits the same way, then PostgreSQL rereads the row A committed and subtracts from it: the final SELECT shows 3000. The last statement puts 5,000 back.

sections.h: Three fixes in the database: subtract in the UPDATE, lock on read, or compare and set
sections.body:
Each fix takes the read-modify-write out of the program's hands, or makes the database check it.

The first fix lets the database do the arithmetic: `UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 1000 WHERE account_id = 109`. This is called an atomic update, because the read and the write happen in one step. The second UPDATE still waits for the first one's row lock. When the lock goes, PostgreSQL rereads row 109 as the first transaction committed it, checks the `WHERE` part again on that version, and subtracts from 4,000. One statement, no extra lock, no retry. Use it whenever the new value can be written in SQL. Other databases have the same idea: MongoDB, a database that stores documents, has `$inc`, and Redis, a database that keeps its data in memory, has `INCRBY`. Many real lost updates come from code that loads a row into an object, changes one field and saves the whole row, where a one-line UPDATE would have done.

The second fix locks the row when you read it. Sometimes the new value needs logic that SQL can't express, such as a fraud score from another program. Then read with `SELECT balance_minor FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 109 FOR UPDATE`. That read takes the same lock an UPDATE would, so the second transaction's read waits until the first commits, and then returns 4,000. PostgreSQL stores a table in blocks of 8 KB called pages, and it writes the lock into the row itself, in a header at the front of the row. So a million locked rows cost no extra memory. A transaction that wants the row sleeps until the holder's transaction ends (lesson 5 builds this). Ask for no more than you need. `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` is enough when you won't delete the row or change its key. Unlike `FOR UPDATE`, it lets through inserts whose foreign key points at the row, such as new payments on a card you've locked. (A foreign key is a column that must match a row in another table, and the database checks that row on every insert.)

The third fix is **compare-and-set**: read without a lock, then write only if the value is still what you read: `UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = 4700 WHERE account_id = 109 AND balance_minor = 5000`. If someone changed the row in between, the `WHERE` no longer matches, the UPDATE changes 0 rows, and the program reads again and tries again. For a row with many fields, a version column does the same job: a number that goes up by one on every change, checked with `AND version = ?`. Libraries that save objects as rows for you, called ORMs, often write exactly that UPDATE.

The Try it shows why compare-and-set works in PostgreSQL. The second compare-and-set waits for the first one's row lock. Then PostgreSQL checks `balance_minor = 5000` against the newly committed version, not the old one. Not every database checks an UPDATE's `WHERE` that way, so check yours before you rely on it.

Prefer the lock for rows that many transactions want at once, where a retry would usually fail again. Prefer compare-and-set for rows that are rarely shared, where a wait would usually be wasted. Next, a fourth fix that leaves the SQL alone.

A's UPDATE prints `UPDATE 1`. B's prints nothing until A commits, then:

sections.h: Repeatable Read catches the lost update in PostgreSQL, and MySQL lets it through
sections.body:
The fourth fix needs no new SQL: run at Repeatable Read, and PostgreSQL notices the race by itself. An isolation level is the setting that decides how much a transaction sees of others running at the same time. At Repeatable Read, a transaction reads from a snapshot, a picture of the committed data taken at its first statement and kept to the end.

Now the fee's UPDATE reaches row 109 and finds a version committed after its snapshot. Read Committed, the default level, would wait and then move on to the new version, as it did for the first fix. Repeatable Read can't, because its snapshot says that version doesn't exist. So PostgreSQL aborts it with `could not serialize access due to concurrent update`. Every PostgreSQL error carries a five-character code, its SQLSTATE, and this one's is 40001. The program then runs the whole transaction again, with the retry loop from What a transaction promises, and the second run reads 4,000.

The rule is called first-updater-wins: the first transaction to change a row keeps it, and a second one running at the same time fails. It catches the bug even when the program writes a plain number, because the check is about the row, not the SQL. Lesson 4 shows where the check lives. Oracle Database, a commercial database that many banks run, does the same at its SERIALIZABLE level and raises ORA-08177. Microsoft's SQL Server does it at its SNAPSHOT level.

MySQL, another free database, doesn't. InnoDB, the part of MySQL that stores the data, gives plain SELECTs a snapshot at its default REPEATABLE READ. But it lets an UPDATE write over the newest committed row without asking whether it changed since the snapshot. In the Try it, the script that fails in PostgreSQL commits in MySQL and loses the payment: the balance ends at 4,700. Hermitage, a set of tests that runs the same races against many databases, marks MySQL's REPEATABLE READ as letting lost updates through. Jepsen, a company that tests databases by breaking them, counted 198 lost updates among 446 transactions in one 2023 test on a single healthy MySQL 8.0.34 server. On MySQL, use one of the first three fixes, or SERIALIZABLE.

**The same level name can make two different promises. Check what yours does before you rely on it.**

Detection also assumes there's one up-to-date copy of the row. Some databases accept writes on several copies at once, on different machines (the Replication track's lessons on many leaders and on leaderless replication). They can't lock a row or compare it with the latest version, and keeping whichever write came last loses updates by design. There the tools are changes that give the same result in any order, such as adding to a counter, and ways to merge two versions. Next, we'll meet the lost update somewhere you might not expect: a to-do list.

In PostgreSQL, the moment A commits, B's UPDATE fails:

```postgresql

```

A's SELECT then shows 4000: the payment stands, and the fee must be run again from its read. In MySQL, B's UPDATE also waits for A's lock, and then succeeds (your time differs):


```text

+---------------+
|          4700 |
+---------------+
```

Two charges of 1,300 in all, and the balance fell by 300. Same level name, same statements: PostgreSQL refused the second write, and MySQL let it erase the first. Each block ends by putting 5,000 back.

sections.h: A to-do list of jobs: claiming one is a read-modify-write too
sections.body:
Some of the company's work shouldn't make a customer wait. It emails receipts, pays each shop what it took that day, and sends some payments to the fraud team for a closer look. So it writes each piece of work as a row in a `jobs` table, a to-do list, and programs called workers do the jobs. A worker loops: find the oldest job that's due, mark it `running`, do the work, mark it `done`. In the course data, five of the eight jobs are `queued` and due, and the oldest is job 2, a fraud review of payment 31. The company runs three workers, so that three jobs run at once.

Claiming a job is a read-modify-write. A worker runs `SELECT job_id ... ORDER BY run_after LIMIT 1` to find the oldest due job (`LIMIT 1` keeps only the first row), then `UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running' ...`. It races every worker that read the same row. The second UPDATE waits for the first, then writes over it. Job 2 ends with `attempts = 2`, and the fraud team reviews payment 31 twice, which is thorough but not what anyone asked for.

The lock fix applies: claim with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. The second worker's read now waits on job 2. When the first worker commits, PostgreSQL rechecks job 2 against the `WHERE` part, sees `running`, and moves on to job 3. No job runs twice. But say each worker keeps its transaction open while it works, so it commits only when its job is done. A fraud review takes 2 seconds, so three workers finish one job every 2 seconds. They all want the same first row.

The workers don't need job 2; any due job will do. `SKIP LOCKED` says exactly that: when another transaction has locked a row, skip it instead of waiting. The claim becomes one statement that picks, locks, marks and returns a job:

```sql
UPDATE jobs
SET status = 'running', locked_by = current_setting('application_name'),
    locked_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1
WHERE job_id = (SELECT job_id FROM jobs
                WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now()
                ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1
                FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING job_id, kind, payload;
```

The inner SELECT finds the job, and `RETURNING` hands back columns of the row the UPDATE changed. Worker 1's inner SELECT locks job 2. Worker 2's skips it and locks job 3, and worker 3's skips both and locks job 5. Nobody waits. `LIMIT 1` keeps each claim to one row. The partial index `jobs_ready_idx`, a sorted list of `run_after` for queued rows only, keeps the search short however many finished jobs pile up. A third option, `NOWAIT`, fails at once with SQLSTATE 55P03 instead of waiting. That suits a request that should answer "this refund is being processed" rather than hang.

Then decide how long a worker holds its job. If it keeps the transaction open while the job runs, the lock works as a lease, a claim that ends by itself when the holder goes away. If the worker's program dies, PostgreSQL rolls back, and the job is `queued` again. That costs one database connection per running job, and an open transaction holds back VACUUM, PostgreSQL's cleanup of old row versions (lesson 4). For anything that calls another company, such as an email provider, claim and commit instead. The work then runs outside any transaction. A second program, the reaper, puts back jobs whose `locked_at` is too old, and the work must be safe to run twice. The worked example builds that worker. Next, we'll see what all this locking costs.

try.title: Three workers, no waiting
steps: Open three terminals in the `labs` folder and run psql in each: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course`. Call them A, B and C: three workers. Start the database first if it isn't running (`docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`).

Name each worker and turn on timing: `SET application_name = 'worker-1';` and `\timing on` in A, the same with `'worker-2'` in B and `'worker-3'` in C. The claim reads that name with `current_setting('application_name')`.

Run `BEGIN;` and the claim in A, then B, then C, without committing. Which job does each get, and does any of them wait? Then run the rest of the block: a NOWAIT test in B, a crash of C (its ROLLBACK), and a new claim in A.

code.title: psql, three sessions on database course

try.expect:
Each claim returns at once with a different job (output trimmed; the times are a few milliseconds, or a couple of hundred on a busy laptop):

```postgresql
-- A
 job_id |     kind     | locked_by
--------+--------------+-----------
      2 | fraud_review | worker-1
-- B
      3 | send_receipt | worker-2
-- C
      5 | settle_merchant | worker-3
```

`pg_stat_activity`, PostgreSQL's list of open sessions, shows nobody waiting: worker-1 is `active` (it is running that query), the other two are `idle in transaction`, and none has `wait_event_type = Lock`. B's NOWAIT test fails at once with `ERROR:  could not obtain lock on row in relation "jobs"` and `55P03`, because job 2 is still queued in B's snapshot but locked by A. After C's ROLLBACK and A's COMMIT, A's new claim returns job 3: B's earlier ROLLBACK put job 3 back, and job 5, freed by C, is next in line. The last statement resets the three jobs.

sections.h: Two transfers that lock in opposite orders wait forever: deadlock
sections.body:
Locking to stop lost updates has a cost of its own. Ivy moves 1,000 from account 109 to 209, while a scheduled transfer moves 3,000 from 209 to 109. Each transfer is two UPDATEs: one takes the money out, one puts it in, and each UPDATE locks its row. Transfer A locks 109. Transfer B locks 209. A's second UPDATE needs 209, so A waits for B. B's second UPDATE needs 109, so B waits for A. Neither can finish. That is a **deadlock**: a ring of transactions, each waiting for a lock that the next one holds. Try it in the simulator: run A's first line, then B's.

PostgreSQL doesn't wait forever. A transaction that has waited for a lock for `deadlock_timeout` (1 second by default) checks who waits for whom. If it finds a ring, it aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE `40P01`, `deadlock detected`, and the other gets its lock and finishes. The cost is a second of waiting and a transaction to run again. The retry loop from What a transaction promises already treats 40P01 like 40001, and lesson 5 builds the detector.

Better to make the ring impossible: every transaction takes its locks in the same order. Sort the two account numbers and lock the lower one first, whichever way the money moves:

```sql
SELECT account_id FROM accounts
WHERE account_id IN (109, 209)
ORDER BY account_id
FOR UPDATE;              -- both transfers lock 109, then 209
```

Now B's first lock request is for 109, which A holds. So B waits while holding nothing, and A finishes. The same rule covers a program that applies a batch of balance changes it received as messages, one row at a time: sort the batch first.

```kotlin
for (change in batch.sortedBy { it.accountId }) {     // every consumer locks in ascending id order
    update.setLong(1, change.amountMinor)
    update.setLong(2, change.accountId)
    update.executeUpdate()                            // holds this row's lock until COMMIT
}
conn.commit()
```

Two more tools belong here. `SET lock_timeout = '2s'` makes any statement that waits longer than that for a lock fail with 55P03, so a stuck holder can't hang a request. And when what you need to put in line isn't a row, use an **advisory lock**, a lock on a number your program picks. Say the company runs several copies of its program, and each night every copy tries to pay shop 1 what it took on 12 June. `SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(1, 20260612)` returns true for the first copy that asks and false for every other, and PostgreSQL releases it at COMMIT. Prefer these `_xact_` functions, whose locks end with the transaction. The session-level `pg_advisory_lock` survives COMMIT. If the program borrows its connections from a pool, a set of open connections it reuses, that lock stays with a connection your code has already handed back.

compare.title: Claiming a job and surviving a deadlock: Oracle and PostgreSQL

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle AI Database 26ai
a.src:
-- 26ai: FETCH FIRST with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is new
SELECT job_id FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= SYSTIMESTAMP
ORDER BY run_after, job_id
FETCH FIRST 1 ROWS ONLY
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

-- older code: open the cursor with no limit and fetch
-- one row; WHERE ROWNUM = 1 ... SKIP LOCKED returns
-- nothing when that one row is already locked

-- FOR UPDATE WAIT 2     wait at most 2 seconds
-- no FOR SHARE or FOR KEY SHARE: row locks are
-- always exclusive

-- deadlock: ORA-00060 rolls back the STATEMENT;
-- the transaction is still open and still holds
-- its other locks until you ROLLBACK

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL 18
b.src:
-- LIMIT with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED since 9.5
SELECT job_id FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now()
ORDER BY run_after, job_id
LIMIT 1
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

-- locking stops once LIMIT has its row, so a locked
-- first row is skipped and the next free one is
-- returned

-- no WAIT n: SET lock_timeout = '2s' (55P03)
-- four modes: FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE,
-- FOR SHARE, FOR KEY SHARE (foreign-key checks)

-- deadlock: 40P01 aborts the whole TRANSACTION;
-- after it only ROLLBACK works, and every lock
-- is released

compare.note: Oracle Database, a commercial database that many banks run, keeps row locks with the rows, as PostgreSQL does, and it has SKIP LOCKED for to-do lists too, so the claim looks almost the same. Three things differ in practice. Limiting the claim: PostgreSQL's LIMIT counts only the rows it managed to lock, while Oracle accepts FETCH FIRST together with FOR UPDATE only since 26ai, so older Oracle code fetches one row at a time from an open-ended SKIP LOCKED query. Lock modes: Oracle has one exclusive row lock, and its foreign-key trap is a different one (a foreign key without an index makes a DELETE of the row it points at lock the whole other table). Deadlocks: PostgreSQL aborts the whole transaction, while Oracle rolls back one statement and leaves the transaction open, so Oracle code must roll back itself before it retries.

worked.title: A receipt worker in Kotlin: claim, commit, work, and a reaper

steps.say: Sending a receipt calls an email company that can take seconds, so this worker uses claim and commit. The claim is its own short transaction: one statement, then COMMIT at once. Commit before the slow part, and nothing stays locked while the email goes out.

The work runs outside any transaction. A second short transaction records the outcome. On failure the job goes back on the list with a delay that grows with each attempt, and after the third attempt it stops at `failed`, like job 6 in the course data.

A worker that dies between the claim and the outcome leaves its job `running` with an old `locked_at`. The reaper puts such jobs back. It is one UPDATE, so it's safe to run in every copy of the program every minute: row locks make each job move once. The `locked_by = ?` in step 2 stops a slow worker from overwriting a job that the reaper already handed to someone else.
steps.code:
-- 3. the reaper: put back jobs whose worker went quiet 10 minutes ago
UPDATE jobs
SET status = CASE WHEN attempts >= 3 THEN 'failed' ELSE 'queued' END,
    locked_by = NULL,
    locked_at = NULL
WHERE status = 'running'
  AND locked_at < now() - interval '10 minutes';

steps.say: Claim and commit means a job can run twice: the worker sent the email, then died before step 2 committed, and the reaper queued the job again. So the email carries a key that stays the same across attempts. The email company drops a second request with the same key, the same way the payments table drops a second `payment_uid` (What a transaction promises).

lab.title: A job queue that never double-claims, and transfers that never deadlock
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the `labs` folder. Six of the ten fail. The tests open real sessions at once (up to six workers) and commit for real, then put the course data back.

`claim_job.sql` is one statement that a worker runs inside its own open transaction. Read the failures: one says a worker waited for another worker's lock, and one shows job 2 claimed twice with `attempts = 2`.
Fix the claim. Add a plain `FOR UPDATE` first and run the tests: the double claim goes away, and the waiting doesn't. Then make it skip what other workers hold.

`transfer.sql` moves money between the two accounts named in a temporary table, `transfer`. Two sessions run it in opposite directions, one statement at a time. Read the log in the failure: it shows the deadlock and the retry. Make every transfer lock its two accounts in the same order before it changes them.
Run the tests until all ten pass. The last one checks that you lock only the two accounts: Ivy's transfer must not wait for Ben's.
hints: Put `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` at the end of the inner SELECT, after `LIMIT 1`. The outer UPDATE then changes a row its own inner SELECT already holds.

For the transfer, add one statement after `BEGIN`: `SELECT a.account_id FROM accounts a, transfer t WHERE a.account_id IN (t.from_account, t.to_account) ORDER BY a.account_id FOR UPDATE OF a;`. `OF a` locks only the account rows.
`LOCK TABLE accounts` also stops the deadlock, and fails the last test: every transfer in the company would wait for every other one.

drill.title: The claim, the compare-and-set and the lock order, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write (1) the statement a worker runs to claim the oldest due queued job from `jobs`, mark it running and return it, so that ten workers at once never wait for each other and never get the same job; (2) a compare-and-set that takes 1,000 from account 109 only if its balance is still the 5,000 you read, and what the program does when it changes 0 rows; and (3) the first statement of a transfer between accounts `:from` and `:to` that makes deadlocks between transfers impossible.

answer.src:
-- 1. the claim
UPDATE jobs
SET status = 'running', locked_by = :worker, locked_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1
WHERE job_id = (SELECT job_id FROM jobs
                WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now()
                ORDER BY run_after, job_id
                LIMIT 1
                FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING job_id, kind, payload;

-- 2. compare-and-set: write only if the value is still the one you read
UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = 4000
WHERE account_id = 109 AND balance_minor = 5000;
-- 0 rows changed: someone got there first. Reload the balance and try again
-- (with a version column: ... AND version = :read_version, SET version = version + 1)

-- 3. lock both accounts, lowest id first, before changing either
SELECT account_id FROM accounts
WHERE account_id IN (:from, :to)
ORDER BY account_id
FOR UPDATE;

recap: A lost update comes from a read-modify-write cycle: two transactions read the same value, each writes a result worked out from it, and the second write erases the first. The row lock makes the second write wait, and it still writes the old result.

Fix it in the database: subtract inside the UPDATE (`SET x = x - n`, the best when it fits), lock the row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` before working out the new value, or compare and set with the old value or a version column, trying again on 0 rows.

PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read notices a lost update (first-updater-wins) and fails the second writer with 40001, so the program runs it again. MySQL's REPEATABLE READ doesn't: the second write wins without an error.

A row lock is a mark kept in the row itself until COMMIT or ROLLBACK, and plain reads never wait for it. Ask for `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` when you won't change the key, so inserts that point at the row can pass.
Claiming a job is a read-modify-write. `FOR UPDATE` stops a job running twice but lines the workers up; `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` lets each take the next free job; `NOWAIT` fails at once with 55P03.

The limit: locks bring deadlocks. Two transactions that lock in opposite orders wait for each other until PostgreSQL aborts one with 40P01, after `deadlock_timeout` (1 s). Lock rows in a fixed order, cap waits with `lock_timeout`, and use advisory locks for things that aren't rows.
closing:
We started with Ivy's account at 40.00 when it should have shown 30.00. Both charges read 50.00, and the lock only made the second one wait to write its out-of-date answer. Any of the four fixes brings the missing 10.00 back: subtract inside the UPDATE, lock on read, compare before writing, or let Repeatable Read refuse.

Look at any code you've written that saves a number: a score, a stock count, a total. If it reads the number, changes it in code and writes it back, two users at once will lose one change.

Next, we'll meet a race that no row lock can stop, because the row that causes it doesn't exist yet.

quiz.q: Three workers claim jobs with `... ORDER BY run_after LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE`, and each keeps its transaction open while its 2-second job runs. Thirty jobs are queued. About how long until all are done, and what brings it near 20 seconds?
options: About 20 seconds already: each worker locks a different row
About 60 seconds, because the workers queue on the same first row; SKIP LOCKED in the claim brings it near 20
About 60 seconds, because PostgreSQL runs one FOR UPDATE per table at a time; more database connections fix it
It never finishes: the three workers deadlock
quiz.why: All three pick the same oldest row, so two wait while one works: one job every 2 seconds, 60 seconds for thirty. With SKIP LOCKED each claim skips rows other workers hold, three jobs run at once, and thirty take about 20 seconds. PostgreSQL has no limit of one row lock per table, and the waits form a line, not a ring, so there is no deadlock.

quiz.q: A program written for PostgreSQL relies on REPEATABLE READ to turn two read-modify-writes of one balance at the same time into 40001 errors, which it retries. The team moves it to MySQL 8.4 and keeps MySQL's default level, also called REPEATABLE READ. What changes?
options: Nothing: both databases follow the same SQL standard level
MySQL reports a deadlock instead of a serialization failure
The second write now commits without an error, and one update is lost
MySQL makes the second transaction's SELECT wait for the first
quiz.why: InnoDB's REPEATABLE READ gives plain SELECTs a snapshot, but an UPDATE writes over the newest committed row without checking whether it changed since that snapshot. The second write waits for the first one's lock and then wins: Hermitage and Jepsen both found lost updates at this level. The name is the same, and the promise isn't. On MySQL, subtract inside the UPDATE, lock the row, or compare and set.

quiz.q: Two programs apply batches of balance changes that they receive as messages, one UPDATE per row, in the order the messages came. A few times a day, one batch fails with SQLSTATE 40P01. What is the best fix?
options: Sort each batch by account_id and apply the updates in that order
Raise deadlock_timeout to 10 seconds so the transactions have time to finish
Run the batches at SERIALIZABLE
Add an index on accounts (account_id)
quiz.why: 40P01 is a deadlock: two batches that touch the same accounts in different orders each hold a row the other needs. If every batch locks in rising account order, a second batch waits at its first shared row while holding nothing, and no ring can form. A longer deadlock_timeout only makes the stuck pair wait longer before PostgreSQL breaks the ring. Serializable adds serialization failures to the deadlocks, and account_id already has an index, because it's the table's key.

quiz.q: A program saves a payment with a version column: `UPDATE payments SET status = 'refunded', version = 8 WHERE payment_id = 31 AND version = 7`. The database reports that 0 rows changed. What happened, and what should the program do?
options: The row was deleted; create it again
PostgreSQL rolled back the transaction; retry the same UPDATE
The UPDATE is still waiting for a lock; wait longer
Another transaction changed the payment since it was read; read it again, redo the change and save again, or report the clash
quiz.why: That UPDATE is compare-and-set: it changes the row only if the version is still the one the program read. 0 rows means someone else committed a change, version 8 or later, in between. (JPA, a common Java library that saves objects as rows, writes this UPDATE for any class with a `@Version` field, and throws `OptimisticLockException` here.) The same UPDATE again would match 0 rows again, because the version it checks is out of date. Read the row again, decide again with what it says now, and save.

quiz.q: What a transaction promises showed that Read Committed allows lost updates. Then why does `UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 100 WHERE account_id = 109`, run by two transactions at once at Read Committed, never lose one?
options: Read Committed turns two updates of one row at the same time into error 40001
The second UPDATE waits for the first one's row lock, then PostgreSQL rereads the newly committed version and subtracts from it
Every single statement runs at SERIALIZABLE
Each statement in autocommit mode locks the whole table
quiz.why: The lost update in that lesson's table comes from working out a value in the program from an earlier read. A subtraction inside the UPDATE does the read and the write in one statement, under the row lock. When the second one gets the lock, Read Committed follows the row to its new version, checks the WHERE again, and subtracts from 4,900. 40001 is what Repeatable Read does, and nothing locks a whole table here.

flashcards.back: Two transactions read the same value and each write a result worked out from it; the second write erases the first. No error is raised.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't `SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 1000` lose updates at Read Committed?
flashcards.back: The second UPDATE waits for the row lock, then PostgreSQL rereads the newly committed version, checks the WHERE again and subtracts from it.

flashcards.front: A compare-and-set UPDATE changes 0 rows. What does it mean?
flashcards.back: Someone changed the row since you read it. Read it again, decide again, and try again.

flashcards.front: What does PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read do with a lost update, and MySQL's?
flashcards.back: PostgreSQL fails the second writer with 40001, could not serialize access due to concurrent update. MySQL lets the second write win without an error.

flashcards.front: Where does PostgreSQL keep a row lock?
flashcards.back: In the locked row itself, in its header on the 8 KB page, not in memory. A transaction waiting for it sleeps until the holder's transaction ends.

flashcards.front: What does `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` do when the first candidate row is locked?
flashcards.back: Skips it and tries the next row, without waiting. With LIMIT 1 it returns the first row it could lock, or none.

flashcards.front: How do you make deadlocks between transfers impossible?
flashcards.back: Lock the rows in one fixed order in every transaction, for example by rising account_id, before changing any of them.

terms.plain: Two read-modify-write cycles on one value at the same time, where the second write erases the first.
Reading a value, working out a new one in the program, and writing it back.
A mark a transaction puts on a row so that other writers wait until it commits or rolls back. Plain reads ignore it.
A write that happens only if the value (or a version number) is still the one you read; otherwise it changes nothing.
Snapshot isolation's rule: of two transactions running at the same time that change the same row, the second one to try fails.
An option on a locking read that skips rows other transactions have locked, instead of waiting for them. Made for to-do lists of jobs.
A ring of transactions, each waiting for a lock the next one holds. PostgreSQL aborts one with 40P01.
A lock on a number the program chooses, to put in line work that isn't a row, such as one daily payment to each shop.

explain_back.prompt: A friend wants to process payouts, the money the company sends each shop, from a PostgreSQL table, with ten copies of a program. Each copy runs `SELECT * FROM payouts_queue WHERE status = 'new' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE`, then calls the bank, then marks the row done, all in one transaction. Explain what will happen when many payouts are waiting, and what you would change.
explain_back.answer: Every copy reads the same oldest row, so one copy gets its lock and nine wait for it. The first copy holds the lock for the whole bank call, maybe a second, so the nine sit idle and then collide again on the next row. No payout goes out twice, which is why tests pass, but ten copies work through the list at the speed of one, and adding copies only adds waiters. I'd add SKIP LOCKED so each copy takes the oldest row nobody holds, and fold the claim into one UPDATE ... WHERE id = (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING. Because a bank call is slow, I wouldn't hold the transaction open across it. I'd commit the claim with a locked_at time, call the bank, and mark the row done in a second short transaction. That needs a reaper for rows stuck in running, and a key on the bank call that stays the same across attempts, because a payout the reaper put back may already have been sent. I'd also check for a partial index on the list's ordering column for status = 'new', so a claim stays quick as finished rows pile up.

deeper.body:
**Four lock strengths.** PostgreSQL has four row lock modes, strongest first. `FOR UPDATE` is taken by DELETE, by an UPDATE that changes a column with a unique index a foreign key could point at, and by `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` is taken by every other UPDATE. `FOR SHARE` lets several transactions hold the row and blocks any change to it. `FOR KEY SHARE` blocks only a DELETE or a key change, and it is what a foreign-key check takes on the row it points at. KEY SHARE conflicts only with FOR UPDATE, so an ordinary UPDATE of a card doesn't block new payments on it, while an explicit `SELECT ... FROM cards WHERE card_id = 5 FOR UPDATE` does. This split arrived in PostgreSQL 9.3; before it, foreign-key checks took SHARE locks and blocked every UPDATE of the row they pointed at. The `pgrowlocks` extension shows the modes on a table's rows.

**MultiXacts.** When several transactions lock one row at once, as the foreign-key checks of many payments on one card do, a single transaction id no longer fits in the row header. PostgreSQL writes a MultiXact id there instead, a pointer to a list of lockers and their modes in `pg_multixact`. MultiXact ids wrap around like transaction ids and need their own freezing (lesson 4).

**Version columns in Java.** JPA, the standard Java way to save objects as rows, and Hibernate, its best-known implementation, turn a field marked `@Version` into compare-and-set: every UPDATE gets `AND version = ?`, and an update that changes no row throws `OptimisticLockException`. A lost update then becomes an exception your code can catch, reload and retry.

**SKIP LOCKED is for to-do lists only.** The PostgreSQL documentation says it gives an inconsistent view of the data, unsuitable for general work but fine for "multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table". Never use it for a report or a balance check: a row you skipped still exists.

**Waking workers.** Asking an empty `jobs` table every 100 ms from ten workers is cheap with the partial index, but `LISTEN` and `NOTIFY` can wake workers instead. The code that inserts a job runs `NOTIFY jobs_ready`, idle workers hold a connection in `LISTEN jobs_ready`, and pgJDBC delivers the notification through `PGConnection.getNotifications()`. Keep the polling as a fallback: a notification sent while a worker restarts is lost.

**Job tables churn.** Every UPDATE writes a new row version (lesson 4). Delete or archive done jobs in batches, or split the table by day and drop old parts, and let autovacuum visit the table more often than its default, which waits until 20% of a table's rows are dead.

**Claims belong at Read Committed.** At Repeatable Read and Serializable, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on a row that another transaction changed and committed after your snapshot fails with 40001 instead of returning the new version. So a claim at those levels turns contention into retries.
